So, each successive sort should not disturb the previous sort.
So, this is called stable sorting.
So, this is obviously desirable because we do it all the time and we really would be
very unhappy if the next round of sorting disturbed our first round of sorting.
So, which of our algorithms is stable?
So, quick sort as shown is not a stable operation.
So, remember that we took the pivot, right.
And in the, at least in our implementation, what we did was we constructed this lower set
and then this upper set to the right of it.
So, this is the picture we had and then finally, and this is the crucial point, we do this
swap.
So, imagine that we have a situation where here we had for example, at this point, Ashwin
with 60 marks and Chandar with also with 60 marks, right.
So, at the point of constructing the lower set, they were in the correct order as in the

But now, after swapping, what happens is that the pivot has come here and Chandar with

So, this, this swapping operation has basically reversed the order of A and C with this vector
with the output was in the input and henceforth therefore, this order will get jumbled.
So, this swap operation during partitioning disturbs the original order, right.
And this also happens in things like selection sort because in selection sort, wherever we
do this long distance thing.
So, remember in selection sort, we picked the minimum and then we exchanged it at the
beginning.
So, if the element at the beginning had the same alphabetical order as, I mean it is
smaller with in the second one, now it moves to a later point in the area and the order
get disturbed.
So, any kind of long distance swapping is very dangerous for stability.
What about Merth sort?
Well, Merth sort would normally be stable provided we all we want is that something to the
right should not go to the left of something in the original value.
So, we do not want some, if we have two elements here and here which are, which should remain
in this order, we do not want them to be exchanged.
Now, why would they be exchanged?
They would be exchanged only if they were equal, right.
That is the only case where stability gets destroyed where equal elements are disturbed
to respect to the previous sorting.

text: order and since Merth sort as we have done is stable, you can also check that similarly
if you do insertion sort carefully, then insertion sort is also stable.
Now, this is not to say that quick sort cannot be made stable is just that the way we have
implemented it, quick sort is not stable.
Another criterion which is related to what we just saw is that we have only concentrated
on the number of steps required in order to compare and exchange to elements.
But, you might want to do other things.
For instance, you might want to penalize movements which take you across large segments
of the array.
So, you might want to say that it is not so good to exchange things far away, it is better
to exchange things near each other.
So, something like bubble sort which we did not look at which only exchange adjacent elements
would be better than something like selection sort which exchange across large intervals.
Now, this could happen if data has a cost and supposing you are sorting an array but this
array is across different, it is so big that it is not stored on a single server.
Then each time you want to swap from one server to another, you could pay an extra cost
which is different.
So, in other words, there might be different criteria which are behind the scenes which
we do not see.
So, imagine when you are sorting something by hand supposing you are sorting a bunch of
heavy cartons, then you can imagine that moving a heavy carton along distance is more expensive
than moving it a short distance.
So, there could be other criteria which govern your cost of sorting which we have not considered
at all in this and people have looked at these things in the literature.
So, very often the question is asked which sort is best?
So, unfortunately it turns out that no single sorting algorithm is always guaranteed to
the best.
It really depends as we said like sorting in the movement and other criteria, some sorting
algorithm may work well in some context, some in another context.
In most memory based context for simple arrays quicksort is the best.
This is why as we said quicksort is usually the default implementation of choice for built-in
sorting algorithms.
Provided we do something intelligent about choosing the pivot and various other things.
On the other hand when we have to move a lot of data, sometimes we cannot store the entire
thing if we are sorting a database, we cannot sort the entire thing in the memory.
So, actually we use a variation of merge sort which is called external merge.
So, it really depends on the context.
Sometimes we use one, sometimes we use another.
If there were a best algorithm, there would be no need to study the other algorithm.
So, the very fact that many of these algorithms are studied shows that in different contexts
you might need to use one or the other idea in order to make things work better.
We have seen merge sort as an order n log n algorithm.
There are other n log n algorithm.
We will see one later on in this course called heap sort.
The main thing to remember is that if we have a naive n squared algorithm which is not
like quicksort, provably n log n in the average case, then this will only work for small
data.
However, sometimes for small data the simplicity of a naive algorithm beats the complexity
of a complicated algorithm.
So, you could even have hybrid algorithms.
You might use divide and conquer when is large and when n becomes small, then you switch
over to maybe insertions.
So there are many different strategies that people use and very often experimentally they
arrive at some combination of strategies.
So, it is not enough to say that one algorithm is the best.
You need to have a good idea about what works and what does not work so that you can tailor
your sorting procedure to suit your requirement.
